method: Each listed item was read with its stem, all options, keyed answer(s), explanations and takeaway. Statuses are manually reasoned, not inferred from a schema or automated pass rule.
limitations: Independent AI editorial/clinical-reasoning screen; not external clinician validation or psychometric validation.
Pass applies only to the recorded content hash. New or changed content requires further review.
No comparison against proprietary examination items; originality judged from author provenance and item content.
Cross-bank learning-objective overlap remains provisional until all batches are available.
Source checks below support only the explicitly associated claims; other category references are general reading unless specifically verified.

items.assessment: New post-procedure sedation makes admission scoring and baseline independence insufficient; current function appropriately drives assistance.
Hip pain after an unwitnessed fall makes assessment and assistance the priority before routine movement or weight bearing; administrative tasks appropriately follow care.
Occult injury assessment in an anticoagulated client is sound, but waiting for bruising and completing only a score are weak advertised shortcuts.
issues: Occult injury assessment in an anticoagulated client is sound, but waiting for bruising and completing only a score are weak advertised shortcuts.
proposedChanges: Use plausible post-fall priorities such as routine observations, medication review or assisted return to bed, with sufficient history to show why injury assessment must come first.

items.assessment: Individualized assessment and assistance are correct, but the key uniquely bundles the plan against alarm-only caricatures.
issues: Individualized assessment and assistance are correct, but the key uniquely bundles the plan against alarm-only caricatures.
proposedChanges: Use concise competing plans such as reassessing pain/toileting, relocating the bed, adjusting alarm sensitivity, or reinforcing call-bell teaching. Explain the ongoing unmet-need assessment rather than hiding every useful action in the key.

items.assessment: Secure nonslip footwear addresses the observed hazard, but an extra aid, all-day inactivity and shuffling without turns are implausible alternatives.
issues: Secure nonslip footwear addresses the observed hazard, but an extra aid, all-day inactivity and shuffling without turns are implausible alternatives.
proposedChanges: Compare actual footwear choices or plausible fit adjustments; label foundation if the task remains direct footwear selection rather than broader clinical reasoning.

items.assessment: Post-fall mechanism review and client planning are appropriate; solely blaming age is a conspicuous strawman.
issues: Post-fall mechanism review and client planning are appropriate; solely blaming age is a conspicuous strawman.
proposedChanges: Use the plausible misconception of retaining the admission plan because measured strength has not changed; explain why the reaching mechanism still reveals a modifiable hazard.

items.assessment: Mobility reassessment after a new field deficit is appropriate; faster walking and permanent walker removal are extreme weak alternatives.
issues: Mobility reassessment after a new field deficit is appropriate; faster walking and permanent walker removal are extreme weak alternatives.
proposedChanges: Use comparable adaptation plans with specific functional cues: doorway/scanning practice, increased assistance with the existing aid, environmental routing, or rehabilitation reassessment. Ensure the best timing/action is unambiguous.

items.assessment: Anticipated toileting assistance fits diuretic-related urgency, but moving the call bell away and continuous bed rest are cartoon unsafe options.
issues: Anticipated toileting assistance fits diuretic-related urgency, but moving the call bell away and continuous bed rest are cartoon unsafe options.
proposedChanges: Compare feasible toileting, education and medication-timing review plans. State the client understands the call bell and requires assistance so the actual service-timing gap decides the answer.

items.assessment: A reliably stabilized transfer surface is needed, but a curtain rail and moving quickly are implausible fixes.
issues: A reliably stabilized transfer surface is needed, but a curtain rail and moving quickly are implausible fixes.
proposedChanges: Use credible equipment alternatives such as relying on the one working brake, asking a helper to stabilize the chair, or requesting a replacement chair; keep the key concise.

items.assessment: Loss of ability to follow instructions changes sit-to-stand suitability; current participation and physical capacity appropriately supersede yesterday plan or weight alone.
Damaged sling removal is correct, but towel repair and holding the tear are cartoon practices.
issues: Damaged sling removal is correct, but towel repair and holding the tear are cartoon practices.
proposedChanges: Compare using the damaged sling for a shorter transfer, choosing an intact but unverified sling, delaying to a scheduled lift, and obtaining a compatible intact replacement. Explain device compatibility as well as integrity.

items.assessment: Compatibility, integrity, assessed staffing, capacity and attachments are relevant system checks; a colour/size label alone does not establish safe compatibility.
Knee buckling during assisted walking requires the trained controlled-descent response and help, rather than arm traction or leaving the client unsupported.
Appropriate repositioning aids are needed when two staff already require excessive force; lifting via bed rails or asking tolerance of a quick lift are weak strawmen.
issues: Appropriate repositioning aids are needed when two staff already require excessive force; lifting via bed rails or asking tolerance of a quick lift are weak strawmen.
proposedChanges: Use plausible alternatives such as adding another manual helper, changing the bed position, using an approved low-friction/device plan or continuing with a different drawsheet grip; make equipment assessment decisive.

items.assessment: Leaving a low-friction device in situ depends on manufacturer guidance and this mobile client sliding risk, not speed, habit or another person experience.
Bedrail reassessment is correct, but telling a climber rails make climbing safe is cartoon content and adding rails without reassessment advertises the error.
issues: Bedrail reassessment is correct, but telling a climber rails make climbing safe is cartoon content and adding rails without reassessment advertises the error.
proposedChanges: Use realistic competing fall plans such as closer observation, a low-bed/environment review, alarm adjustment or continuing full rails. Specify the question is selecting the safer overall plan after climbing occurs.

items.assessment: Assessing pain/confusion and less restrictive options is correct in the stated nonemergency situation; family holding arms continuously is implausible.
issues: Assessing pain/confusion and less restrictive options is correct in the stated nonemergency situation; family holding arms continuously is implausible.
proposedChanges: Replace with a credible alternative such as requesting a sedating PRN or using a protective dressing cover; ensure context distinguishes cause assessment from premature restrictive treatment.

items.assessment: Authorized restraint still requires ongoing need review, neurovascular/skin checks and basic care; deferring toileting neglects continuing needs.
New cool pale fingers indicate possible compromised perfusion; immediate safe relief and assessment take precedence over routine documentation or warming.
Individual supervision and environmental controls fit traffic-related elopement risk, but keeping all residents in bed is absurdly broad.
issues: Individual supervision and environmental controls fit traffic-related elopement risk, but keeping all residents in bed is absurdly broad.
proposedChanges: Use plausible resident-specific measures such as family visit scheduling, an exit reminder, a door alarm or assigned supervision; provide enough context to distinguish reliable protection from adjuncts.

items.assessment: An unexpectedly missing cognitively impaired resident requires immediate coordinated response; sequential lone search or family calls can delay protection.
Prepared equipment, hazard reduction and a shared response plan are useful; mouth insertion is a recognizable seizure-safety misconception, not an arbitrary distractor.
Immediate protection and assistance during an active seizure is appropriate and honestly labelled foundation; oral water and restraint are common harmful first-aid misconceptions.
Onset and duration characterize the ongoing event and guide urgent escalation; aura, trigger and family history questions are useful later but not equivalent here.
Immediate rescue is correct, but collecting valuables and an incident report are far weaker than real competing emergency tasks.
issues: Immediate rescue is correct, but collecting valuables and an incident report are far weaker than real competing emergency tasks.
proposedChanges: Compare rescuing the immediately endangered client with alarm activation, containment and extinguisher use. The stem already states help is being summoned, which can make rescue the defensible immediate priority.

sourceCheckNote: This slice reviewed for clinical coherence, conservative safety principles and item quality; no new item-specific external clinical verification is claimed.
